Best US Stocks to Buy Now: 5 S&P 500 Stocks That Could Be Bargains After the Sell-Off
article:
Fears over rising bond yields and the return on
AI investment
have pressured share prices, at least for some companies, creating uncertainty for investors.
However, market corrections can also provide opportunities to invest in quality businesses at more reasonable valuations.
The key is identifying companies with strong fundamentals, durable competitive advantages and attractive long-term growth prospects.
This article will take a closer look at five
S&P 500 stocks
that have suffered a decline of at least 10% over the past month (as at 30 October 2026).
Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META) – The Mega-Cap Growth Stock
Meta’s shares fell 15.3% in October, with investors concerned over the costs of its AI investments and legal troubles (the latter include a US$25 billion fine imposed by a judge in New Mexico).
Although investors were excited over the rapid uptake of Meta’s Muse agent, questions remain over whether the returns will justify the company’s massive AI investments.
In fact, the company’s recently released figures for 3Q2026 showed free cash flow going negative.
However, the company’s core advertising business is still going strong.
In 3Q2026, revenue grew 26% year on year, although the operating margin halved to 20%, partly because of legal costs.
Looking ahead, Meta’s ability to monetise its AI business remains key, and this will depend on how much value it can extract from consumers (from advertising, subscription fees, commissions etc.), and what percentage of its 3.6 billion daily active user base it can activate.
Meta also faces various legal and regulatory challenges, including the August 2026 agreement to resolve litigation related to teen mental health, which provides for US$18.6 billion in settlements.
These could end up becoming a recurring cost of doing business, and not just one-offs.
AT&T Inc (NYSE: T) – The Undervalued Consumer Giant
AT&T’s stock is down by 11.9% over the past month, amid concerns that
Starlink
, the satellite internet service of
SpaceX
(NASDAQ: SPCX), will muscle in on the telco business.
Despite the decline, the company’s business is performing decently, especially for a mature telco.
Overall revenue for the first 9 months of 2026 was 3.5% higher than a year earlier, reaching over US$95 billion.
Notably, its advanced connectivity segment, which aims to provide subscribers with both 5G and fibre coverage, is growing faster than the overall business.
The company expects to generate over US$18 billion in free cash flow in 2026, rising to over US$21 billion in 2028.
This will provide it with plenty to return to shareholders, whether in the form of dividends or share buybacks.
The telco is currently trading at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of just 8.3x, compared to 12.6x in March this year.
This could prove to be a bargain, but only if Starlink proves to be less of a threat than feared.
Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU) – The AI / Semiconductor Opportunity
Micron, one of the big 3 memory
chipmakers
globally, has seen its shares fall by 19.4% over the past month, as investors question how sustainable the AI boom is.
This sell-off comes despite the company’s strong financial performance.
Revenue for its financial year ending September 2026 (FY2026) was up 256% to US$133 billion.
Net income rose to 9.1 times its FY2025 level, reaching US$87 billion.
The company expects its FY2027 performance to be even stronger, as industry demand has actually gone up over the past quarter.
However, many of these gains appear to be already priced in as Micron’s share price rose 884% between January 2025 and October 2026, making investors nervous at the slightest hint of turbulence in AI-driven demand.
There’s also the spectre of more competition.
Currently, the global market for memory chips is an oligopoly – Micron,
Samsung Electronics
(KRX: 005930) and
SK Hynix
(KRX: 000660) accounted for 87% of global DRAM market share in 2Q2026.
But new competitors, such as China’s
ChangXin Memory Technologies
(SSE: 688825), or CXMT, may disrupt the market, resulting in lower margins.
The Charles Schwab Corporation (NYSE: SCHW) – The Financial Blue Chip
Charles Schwab is a leading investment services firm with over US$13 trillion in client assets.
Its shares are down by over 10% in the past month.
The stock has declined, in part, because of fears that AI agents will be able to help investors trade, disrupting the business model of incumbents such as Charles Schwab.
The company continues to deliver strong financial performance.
Revenue of US$20.7 billion in the first nine months of 2026 (9M2026) was 18% higher than a year ago, while net income rose by 28% to US$8.1 billion.
Schwab is not waiting for AI to eat its lunch.
It recently launched Charley, an AI-powered assistant to provide clients with conversational access to tools and insights.
Schwab also serves Registered Investment Advisors (RIAs) in the US and has partnered with Anthropic to bring Claude to these RIAs.
These initiatives, along with its brand name and long track record, should enable Schwab to adapt and thrive in this new AI era.
Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ: GOOG) – The Quality Compounder
Alphabet has declined by 16.9% over the past month, as investors grew concerned about its high AI spend, as well as the cannibalisation of its higher-margin search business by its lower-margin AI search feature.
Alphabet reported negative free cash flow (FCF) of US$9.1 billion in 3Q2026, its second consecutive quarter in the red.
However, top-line growth is actually accelerating.
In 3Q2026, revenue was 25% higher than a year ago, compared to 16% in 3Q2025.
If the company is able to keep growing revenue, this might offset margin declines, allowing the absolute level of profits to continue rising.
Alphabet remains one of the best-placed enterprises to navigate the AI era, with a unique combination of cloud, AI, and advertising businesses that can benefit from the technology.
One potential game-changer that the market may not be paying enough attention to is its business selling tensor processing unit (TPU) chips, its homegrown AI chip system, which was once reserved for internal use but is now being sold directly to customers.
The value of the TPU business has been estimated at US$900 billion, which would make a meaningful contribution to Alphabet’s current US$3.4 trillion market capitalisation.
Get Smart: Buy Quality Businesses, Not Just Falling Share Prices
Market sell-offs can provide opportunities to invest in strong companies at more attractive valuations.
Investors should assess earnings resilience, cash generation, competitive advantages and valuation before making a decision.
Not all AI “winners” will survive this cycle.

title: STI’s Red October 2026: 4 Blue-Chip REITs Still in the Green
article:
Singaporeans know how it feels when the transboundary haze settles over the island.
October brought a different kind of haze for investors, as Singapore’s blue chips came under pressure.
But four
real estate investment trusts
(REITs) managed to rise above the gloom, delivering positive returns despite the downturn.
The
SPDR STI ETF
(SGX: ES3), an ETF that mimics Singapore’s
Straits Times Index
(SGX: ^STI), delivered a negative 5.5% return for October 2026.
Over the same period,
Frasers Centrepoint Trust
(SGX: J69U), or FCT, delivered a 3.5% total return.
CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust
(SGX: C38U), or CICT,
Frasers Logistics & Commercial Trust
(SGX: BUOU), or FLCT, and
Mapletree Logistics Trust
(SGX: M44U), or MLT, returned 2.2%, 1.7% and 0.9%, respectively.
Stock
Ticker
October 2026 Total Return
SPDR STI ETF
SGX: ES3
-5.5%
Frasers Centrepoint Trust (FCT)
SGX: J69U

SGX: C38U

Frasers Logistics & Commercial Trust (FLCT)
SGX: BUOU

Mapletree Logistics Trust (MLT)
SGX: M44U
+0.9%
Source: Fiscal.ai.
These are total returns, which include distributions and not just unit price movements.
The gains may appear modest, but they still stand in stark contrast to the STI’s dip.
So what helped them weather the
downturn
?
Their latest business updates offer some clues.
What drove FCT’s record payout?
FCT
owns a portfolio of eight suburban malls in Singapore.
For the fiscal year ended 30 September 2026 (FY2026), net property income (NPI) rose 15.7% year on year (YoY) to S$321.7 million.
A full year’s contribution from Northpoint City’s South Wing provided the biggest boost.
Distribution per unit (DPU) climbed 2.0% to a record S$0.12350, while second-half DPU grew 2.6% YoY to S$0.06214.
Retail committed occupancy stood at 99.7%, excluding NEX, which is currently undergoing an asset enhancement initiative (AEI).
Rental reversions came in at 6.6%, while the average cost of debt fell to 3.2% from 3.8% a year ago.
However, the results were not entirely rosy.
Distributions from joint ventures fell 11.7% YoY, as a one-off special distribution from the previous year did not recur.
Tenant sales growth was also modest at just 1.3%.
Where is Singapore’s largest REIT finding growth?
CICT had a strong third quarter of 2026 (3Q2026), with NPI rising 13.8% YoY to S$334.9 million.
As CICT pays distributions half-yearly, there was no DPU this quarter.
New assets drove the growth.
CICT acquired Paragon on 1 July 2026, while Gallileo in Frankfurt and its increased stake in CapitaSpring also contributed to the stronger performance.
Integrated development NPI climbed 40.8% YoY.
There were also some encouraging signs across the portfolio.
Committed occupancy improved from 95.6% to 96.1% over the quarter, while nine-month rental reversions came in at 4.6% for retail and 7.1% for office properties.
The average cost of debt also eased to 2.8%.
However, not everything was moving in the right direction.
Retail NPI fell 8.2% YoY, while aggregate leverage climbed to 39.7%.
Can logistics make up for FLCT’s business park problem?
FLCT has 114 properties spread across five countries.
It reports financial results only twice a year, so its latest business update for the third quarter of the fiscal year ending 30 September 2026 (3QFY2026) did not include NPI or DPU figures.
Overall portfolio occupancy was 96.1%, while its logistics and industrial (L&I) business was a bright spot, with occupancy at 99.7%.
Rental reversions for these properties also came in at a healthy 11.9%.
The trust also expanded its logistics portfolio, acquiring four freehold properties in Germany and the Netherlands for around S$441.5 million.
Management expects the deal to lift DPU by 1.7%.
But the picture was less encouraging for its commercial properties.
Commercial rental reversions were -0.3%, while nine leases at Alexandra Technopark were renewed at rents 3.6% below their previous rates.
For now, FLCT’s L&I properties appear to be doing the heavy lifting.
Is China still weighing on MLT?
MLT owns 172 logistics properties, but its latest results point to relatively modest growth.
For the second quarter of the fiscal year ending 31 March 2027 (2QFY2027), NPI rose 1.0% YoY to S$154.8 million, while DPU edged up 0.1% to S$0.01816.
There was some improvement in rental reversions, which picked up to 2.1% from 0.9% in the previous quarter.
However, China remained a weak spot, with rental reversions still at -1.7%, compared with 4.2% excluding China.
MLT also divested around S$243 million worth of assets during the current fiscal year, at an average 3.1% premium to valuation.
Distributions to perpetual securities holders rose 33.6% YoY.
Aggregate leverage fell to 37.5% from 40.5%, although this was partly due to MLT temporarily using proceeds from perpetual securities to repay debt.
What did these four REITs have in common?
Occupancy across all four portfolios stayed above 96%, while rental reversions were positive in most parts of their portfolios.
Asset sales tested valuations.
FLCT sold its long-vacant Juniper building 37.5% above book value, and MLT’s divestments fetched a premium.
To put it simply, these REITs kept most of their buildings full and most of their rents rising.
In a volatile month, that may have given investors some reassurance.
Get Smart: Ask how the next deal gets paid for
One month of outperformance tells you little about the next twelve.
Gearing, however, offers clearer information.
FCT’s White Sands proceeds will cut aggregate leverage from 38.7% to 36.8%.
The other three REITs are closer to the 40% mark.
CICT’s aggregate leverage stands at 39.7%, while MLT’s pro forma gearing, which assumes the November 2026 redemption of its older perpetual securities, would be 40.4%.
FLCT’s leverage will reach about 38.7% once its acquisition settles.
That leaves S$547 million of headroom, down from S$727 million a quarter ago.
But why does this matter?
A REIT with limited borrowing headroom may need to issue new units to fund its next acquisition.
New units can dilute DPU.
Before you buy any of them, check the gearing and ask how management plans to pay for the next deal.

title: Japan’s Nikkei poised to enter bear market as AI selloff deepens
article:
(Nov 6): Japan’s Nikkei 225 Stock Average slumped Friday, putting the tech-heavy gauge on course to enter a technical bear market as investors unwind artificial intelligence-related trades.

The Nikkei fell as much as 7.1% to 56745.81, breaking under the closely watched 60,000 level and putting it 20% below the peak reached in June. The broader Topix index declined as much as 6.4%, the most since April 2025. Cable maker Furukawa Electric Co and semiconductor company Rohm Co slid more than 10%.

The weakness in Tokyo followed a post-election drop on Wall Street, where falls in chipmakers snowballed as investors bailed from technology shares on speculation that Democrats will clamp down on the artificial intelligence industry. Moves in Japan were also mirrored in South Korea and Taiwan, which saw sharp selloffs.

“Today’s market has the appearance of ‘panic selling,’” said Jumpei Tanaka, head of investment strategy at Pictet Asset Management Japan. “We are at the ‘brink’ of whether the AI rally is heading toward its end or is merely a temporary pause.”

Markets across the region saw selling in tech stocks with those such as Taiwan’s Taiex on course to also enter a technical bear market, down 20% from its peak levels. South Korea’s Kospi, which includes names such as Samsung Electronics Co and SK Hynix Inc has plunged as much as 8.8%.

See also: Thai spyware alerts prompt opposition leaders to demand probe

While stocks took a hit, investors looked toward safer assets. Japan’s five-year bond yield fell 10.5 basis points to 2.085% while the yen rose past 158 to the dollar.

The Nikkei’s significant drop from June has featured a sharp deterioration in sentiment for formerly high-flying stocks. Kioxia Holdings Corp, which had at one point been the world’s best performer and Japan’s most valuable company, has plunged more than 70% from its record high.

“AI semiconductor stocks have been moving violently lately, which has made them a hard asset to invest in,” said Kazuki Sawamura, strategist at Shinkin Asset Management. “Since the US economy and corporate earnings are solid, I would also expect that investors will keep seeking other stocks while AI semiconductor stocks are unstable.”

title: Brent oil set for biggest weekly loss since 2020 on war hopes
article:
(Nov 6): Brent oil was on track for its biggest weekly loss since April 2020 after a volatile stretch of trading, as investors weighed prospects for an end to the months-long war in the Middle East.

The global benchmark climbed to trade near US$99 a barrel on Friday, extending a rebound from a sharp sell-off following a Democratic sweep of the US midterm elections. Despite the gains, front-month futures are down about 16% this week. They rolled from December at the start of the week, with the January contract itself falling almost 13% over the same period.

While there are hopes for a faster end to the conflict, major differences remain. Tehran wants a US naval blockade of its ports lifted, sanctions eased and frozen assets released before fully reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Still, The New York Times reported Iran is reviewing proposals about its nuclear programme presented by mediators, suggesting recent diplomatic efforts by Qatar to prevent a resumption of full military conflict are having some success.

Brent rallied in October to a six-month high as US President Donald Trump threatened renewed strikes on Iran following the midterms. For now, he is showing restraint, while Democratic control of both houses of Congress may constrain the administration’s ability to conduct further military action.

“What matters is whether the White House changes its strategy towards Iran,” said Pavel Molchanov, an analyst at Raymond James & Associates Inc. He said a durable diplomatic settlement that reopens Hormuz could push oil prices even lower, but cautioned that “we ought to remain sceptical”.

Trump met with his national security advisers to discuss Iran on Thursday as part of his weekly intelligence meeting, Axios reported, citing two unnamed US officials. He is considering three options: new strikes, continuing efforts to hobble Tehran economically, or cutting a deal that includes significant concessions to the Iranians, the report said.

See also: Oil extends slide after plunging 8% on hopes to end US-Iran war

Despite frequent attacks on vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz, there has been a revival in crude exports from the Persian Gulf. That has prompted Saudi Arabia to cut prices for buyers in Asia from levels already at a six-year low, as producers compete for market share.

Still, oil-product exports from the Gulf remain constrained. Those disruptions, along with escalating Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, have helped to drive prices higher. Before the midterms, Trump and President Vladimir Putin struck a deal to release Russian diesel into global markets, part of efforts by the US president to tame soaring prices.

A tanker carrying Russian diesel could arrive in New York on Saturday, according to ship-tracking data. The US Treasury last month issued a waiver allowing flows of the Russian fuel to the country until next April.

See also: IEA issues warning on gas market tightness extending into 2027

title: Malaysian bonds lure buyers as oil squeezes peers, analysts say
article:
(Nov 6): Malaysia’s status as a net energy exporter is bolstering the appeal of its sovereign debt, analysts say, shielding the market from regional inflation pressures even as global oil prices fluctuate.

A Bloomberg index tracking Malaysian sovereign bond returns has risen 0.2% so far this year, outpacing regional peers like Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines. The ringgit has also gained 0.3% against the dollar in 2026, compared with declines in the Philippine peso, Indonesian rupiah, and Thai baht.

Driving that outperformance is a subdued inflation backdrop. Malaysia’s consumer prices accelerated just 1.8% in September from a year earlier, the slowest pace among major Southeast Asian economies, anchoring local bond yields. Domestic fuel subsidies have kept consumer price pressures contained. At the same time, state coffers receive a lift from rising energy prices through higher dividends from state-owned oil and gas firm Petroliam Nasional Bhd (PETRONAS), easing pressure on the government to issue more debt.

“Malaysia’s bonds are better positioned than Southeast Asian peers if oil prices remain elevated,” said Winson Phoon, head of fixed‑income research at Maybank Securities. “Malaysia enjoys the twin advantages from its net energy and electric and electronic exports, which support the fiscal balance and current account surplus position.”

An auction of 10-year Malaysian benchmark bonds on Oct 29 drew a bid-to-cover ratio of 2.58 times, the strongest demand for a long-bond sale since June, following robust interest in a 2029 note earlier in the month, according to Bloomberg calculations of official data. By contrast, a 10-year auction in the Philippines, a net importer grappling with high energy prices, drew a bid-to-cover of 2.01 times, its lowest since June.

See also: Anwar: There was corporate mafia 25 years ago

Citigroup Inc holds an overweight position on 10-year Malaysian government bonds in its model emerging-market debt portfolio, strategists including Rohit Garg and Gordon Goh wrote in a note last week. They anticipate limited fiscal fallout from government subsidies.

Bank Negara Malaysia left its benchmark interest rate unchanged on Thursday, though it signalled readiness to act if emerging price pressures start to build.

title: The evolving role of energy players in powering AI
article:
The scale and speed of artificial intelligence (AI) deployment have accelerated in recent years. As AI adoption grows, so does demand for the physical infrastructure behind it, from data centres to semiconductors.

However, powering AI growth and the digital economy is becoming increasingly complex, as the energy ecosystem balances energy security, energy equity and environmental sustainability.

Energy providers are increasingly required to enhance their capabilities to deliver energy solutions that support customers’ increasingly complex needs. Being solely a power supplier is no longer enough; customers now seek partners for integrated solutions.

The rise of AI and energy demand

According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), a ChatGPT prompt uses nearly 10 times the energy of a conventional Google search. This means power demand from data centre servers is climbing as rising AI usage increases computing workloads.

As AI gains mass adoption, the IEA estimates data centres will account for 3% of global electricity demand, or 950 terawatt-hours (TWh) by 2030. This is double the 2024 level.

Operating 24/7, data centres require reliable baseload power to function and support AI deployment. Similarly, as advanced manufacturing firms, including semiconductor fabs, expand capacity to fulfil orders driven by AI demand for computing capabilities, they seek stable power sources.

Against a backdrop of increasing demand from the AI-driven economy for resilient energy sources, energy providers are strengthening procurement and securing their generation capacity.

Recognising the evolving energy landscape, Sembcorp Industries has been augmenting its capabilities to meet AI-driven demand and power digital infrastructure, especially in its home market of Singapore.

This has positioned Sembcorp as a key provider to Singapore’s fast-growing digital economy. Today, Sembcorp supplies close to one-third of the electricity demand from Singapore’s data centre and semiconductor sectors.

These customers have signed long-term power contracts with the company to power their operations, including data centre players such as Equinix, ST Telemedia Global Data Centres and Singapore Telecommunications (Singtel).

Besides data centres, semiconductor manufacturer Micron Technology increased its electricity purchases from Sembcorp with an additional 150 megawatt (MW) power purchase agreement earlier this year, bringing total contracted supply capacity to 600MW and reinforcing Sembcorp’s leadership in Singapore’s energy landscape.

The firm’s generation capacity underpins customers’ confidence. Recently boosted by a new 600MW hydrogen-ready combined-cycle gas turbine plant on Jurong Island, Sembcorp’s total gas-fired and renewables portfolio is now 5.7 gigawatts (GW) in Singapore. This capacity is further augmented by regional renewable energy import opportunities totalling more than 2GW.

As AI-driven power demand grows, customers are also seeking more sustainable ways to power their operations.

Singapore, which generates 95% of its electricity from gas, is one market which has recognised the impact of data centres on the energy system and its net-zero goal. To address energy demand and sustainability concerns, the Singapore government added energy efficiency and sustainability criteria to its Second Data Centre – Call for Application (DC-CFA2) exercise.

Energy decarbonisation is thus another layer of consideration impacting the energy landscape and energy-purchasing decisions. Power generation must be robust, reliable, and sustainable.

Recognising this reality, Sembcorp has diversified its energy generation mix to better support the increasingly complex needs of next-generation data centres.

Since 2020, the company has grown gross renewable energy capacity from 2.6GW to 21.9GW across Southeast Asia, Australia, China, India, the Middle East and the UK. Including projects under construction, Sembcorp owns 4.3 gigawatt-hour (GWh) of energy storage systems.

Sembcorp is Singapore’s largest renewable energy player with over 1 gigawatt-peak (GWp) of renewable energy capacity. It also operates the country’s largest energy storage system. At 326 megawatt-hours (MWh), the Jurong Island facility supports Singapore’s growing solar deployment, addressing intermittency and enhancing grid reliability.

Equipped with multiple generation sources, spanning gas, renewables, energy storage, and electricity imports, Sembcorp can offer integrated solutions tailored to customers’ energy needs. For example, its agreements with global data centre company Equinix encompass 133.5 megawatt-peak (MWp) of solar capacity and 30MW of gas-fired generation, illustrating Sembcorp’s ability to combine different energy sources to support the reliability and decarbonisation needs of digital infrastructure.

Beyond supplying reliable and sustainable energy to fuel AI-related growth, Sembcorp’s deep engineering expertise enables it to be more than just an energy supplier. Sembcorp recently signed separate memoranda of understanding (MoUs) with DayOne Data Centers and Singtel subsidiary Nxera Singapore to explore energy solutions for data centre deployment.

By bringing its technical and energy expertise into customers’ planning earlier, Sembcorp can work alongside them as requirements evolve and operations grow. This is redefining the role of a power generator — from an energy supplier to a long-term strategic energy partner.

Besides expanding its energy portfolio to meet rising energy and sustainability imperatives, energy generators must actively future-proof their businesses. To that end, Sembcorp is exploring several initiatives to capture future opportunities.

One area gaining momentum is biomethane, particularly as demand for greener energy solutions grows.

Sembcorp was recently appointed one of three approved aggregators in Singapore’s biomethane regulatory sandbox. Under the initiative, Sembcorp will import up to 7.18 trillion British thermal units of biomethane annually, equivalent to approximately 120MW of electricity generation capacity.

This could not be timelier for data centre developers. Under DC-CFA2, operators are required to source for at least 50% of their power from green energy, and biomethane is an approved green energy pathway.

Emerging technologies could open up entirely new possibilities for Singapore’s energy mix. With nuclear energy regaining policy attention, Sembcorp is preparing itself for the possibility of nuclear power deployment in Singapore. To this end, it has signed separate MoUs with nuclear engineering solutions provider AtkinsRéalis and ST Engineering to exchange knowledge on nuclear energy and explore potential cooperation.

Singapore’s future energy mix could also increasingly extend beyond its shores. To complement local power generation, the Energy Market Authority of Singapore granted Sembcorp conditional approval to import up to 1.3GW of renewable electricity into its home market through a power corridor linking Singapore, Malaysia and Vietnam.

Taken together, these initiatives reflect how the energy landscape is broadening as new technologies emerge and AI-driven demand accelerates. For energy generators, staying relevant will mean evolving beyond existing models and developing the capabilities to respond to new sources of demand, while navigating the equally important imperatives of energy security and sustainability.

Not resting on its laurels, Sembcorp continues to broaden and deepen its capabilities to help power Singapore’s next phase of AI-driven growth, while advancing energy security and sustainability and reimagining the role and capabilities of power generators.

title: Asian stocks brace for selloff as AI rout deepens
article:
(Nov 6) : Asian stock futures pointed to steep losses on Friday as a post-election rout in chipmakers deepened on Wall Street on growing concerns that Democrats will seek tighter regulation of the artificial intelligence industry.

Equity-index futures for South Korea and Taiwan, home to some of the world’s largest chipmakers, fell at least 7%, while those for Japan sank almost 6%. Futures for Australia and Hong Kong pointed to more modest losses.

In the US, the S&P 500 plunged 4.4% to mark its worst performance since the April 2025 tariff meltdown. The Nasdaq 100 slid 6.4%, wiping out US$2.3 trillion in value as it capped its worst session since March 2020. A closely-watched gauge of chip giants tumbled 12%, with Nvidia Corp., Qualcomm Inc. and Arm Holdings Plc among the biggest decliners. Elon Musk-led Tesla Inc. and SpaceX slid over 9%.

Elsewhere, Treasuries and the dollar rose as investors rushed to haven assets, with the yield on the two-year note falling 12 basis points to 4.46%. Gold climbed for a second day on Thursday, while Bitcoin sank.

Global financial markets have been whipsawed this week as investors initially bet that the Democratic sweep of Congress in midterms would hasten an end to the Iran war, while fears grew of tighter regulation of the data-center industry. A gauge of semiconductor makers has slumped almost 16% this week, putting it on track for its worst weekly performance since April last year.

The data-center slowdown due to the political shift is going to be real, and the earnings estimates behind the valuations that were the cornerstone of bullish arguments are no longer valid, according to Michael O’Rourke at JonesTrading.

See also: S&P 500 sinks 4% as AI washout rattles Wall Street

“Investors have no idea where those estimates will reset,” he said. “As a result, they are de-risking until clarity returns, which won’t be for some time.”

In Asia, Korean chipmakers Samsung Electronics Co. and SK Hynix Inc., along with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. have borne the brunt of the AI-related selloff. In contrast, Hong Kong stocks have rallied as investors rotated away from AI supply chain stocks into discounted Chinese internet platforms.

On the economic front, weekly jobless claims fell below all estimates, Labor Department data show. Investors will be looking to the US payrolls report on Friday for more clues on the path for interest rates.

See also: Stocks, bonds climb after US election as oil sinks

Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Beth Hammack said rates need to be restrictive to bring inflation to the central bank’s target, and more frequent moves can reduce the risk that policy falls behind.

title: S&P 500 sinks 4% as AI washout rattles Wall Street
article:
(Nov 6) : A post-election slide in chipmakers snowballed as investors bailed from technology shares on speculation that congressional Democrats will clamp down on the artificial-intelligence industry.

In its worst session since March 2020, the Nasdaq 100 sank 6.4%, wiping out US$2.3 trillion in value. The S&P 500 fell 4.4%. A key gauge of chip giants tumbled 12%. Qualcomm Inc. and Arm Holdings Plc’s sank on underwhelming outlooks. Apple Inc. raised US$7.5 billion from its high-grade bond offering, adding to a flurry of tech issuance. Tesla Inc. and SpaceX slid at least 9%.

Wall Street’s selloff easily erased a rally on Wednesday, when the sweep of Congress by Democrats sent oil sharply lower on bets the election would speed an end to the Iran war. But even as broad stock benchmarks soared in that session, signs of unease toward the AI trade were evident.

The data-center slowdown due to the political shift is going to be real, and the earnings estimates behind the valuations that were the cornerstone of bullish arguments are no longer valid, according to Michael O’Rourke at JonesTrading.

“Investors have no idea where those estimates will reset,” he said. “As a result, they are de-risking until clarity returns, which won’t be for some time.”

A rotation toward defensive sectors morphed into a broader equity rout, with a gauge of volatility spiking. Bitcoin sank. In a rush for safety, bonds rose despite higher oil prices. Fading enthusiasm for investment in the AI buildout prompted investors to trim bets on Federal Reserve hikes.

See also: Stocks, bonds climb after US election as oil sinks

Michael Burry, who made his name shorting the US housing market, said he sold 25% of his put positions in the US$58 billion VanEck Semiconductor ETF amid a deepening rout in US technology stocks. “The SMH put positions even after the sale however have become very large positions,” he wrote.

Thursday’s action is what happens when euphoria and hype become the reason why stocks go up, rather than fundamentals, according to David Bahnsen at The Bahnsen Group. The rout is also an important reminder the S&P 500 is “way too concentrated” in tech stocks, he added.

Where this differs from a regular selloff is that we are not seeing recoveries after significant losses, such as Intel Corp. falling further this week even after plunging almost 30% Friday, according to Jakub Rochlitz at eToro. There’s also increasing cross-sector correlation and a rise in volatility, meaning that the rout is spreading across the market.

See also: Asian tech stocks to rise on AI rally amid US votes

“The all-or-nothing mentality is surprising to us, because we believe the real truth is more nuanced,” said Chris Zaccarelli at Northlight Asset Management. “We do agree that sentiment has shifted and building data centers will become more difficult, but if there is a productive business case for building them, then they will get built.”

Wavering AI optimism is affecting rates through expectations for growth and Fed policy — neither of which will depend much on Friday’s jobs report, according to Will Compernolle at FHN Financial.

“If there truly is a sharp pullback in AI investment, the labor market impacts could be minimal — the capital intensity has meant few jobs added during the surge, so likewise few should be lost through any decline,” he said. “If an investment pullback eventually ripples into the broader economy through financial contagion, it won’t be revealed tomorrow.”

title: Chips selloff worsens as fears about AI trade grip stock market
article:
(Nov 6): Shares of semiconductor stocks plunged on Thursday, extending a recent selloff as investors turn sceptical on the artificial intelligence (AI) trade after the Democrats dominated the midterm elections.

The Philadelphia Stock Exchange Semiconductor Index was down 9.2%, putting it on pace for its worst day since June. The index, known as the SOX, is down about 12% this week, which would be its worst performance since April 2025, and is on track for a fifth straight weekly drop, its longest streak since then.

Democrats took control of the Senate and House of Representatives in Tuesday’s midterm elections, with many voters indicating their opposition to data centres. In Texas, governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has called for an immediate moratorium on data centre development.

Data centres are a critical component of AI infrastructure, and they are filled with racks of semiconductors. Should spending on data centres slow, it would have massive ramifications for chipmakers over the coming years.

Among notable movers, Nvidia Corp fell as much as 7.5%, the worst intraday drop since April 2025. Advanced Micro Devices Inc slumped 15%, Micron Technology Inc lost 13%, Broadcom Inc dropped 7.2% and Intel Corp dropped 9.2%. Meanwhile, Qualcomm Inc tumbled 10% in the wake of disappointing results, while Arm Holdings plc shed 13% on its own report.

See also: Apple seeks about US$7 bil from first bond sale in over a year — Bloomberg

The selloff extended beyond chipmakers to other parts of the trade. Memory storage companies Western Digital Corp and Seagate Technology Holdings plc slid more than 14%, and so-called neocloud companies CoreWeave Inc and Nebius Group NV were down significantly as well.

However, not everyone on Wall Street is throwing in the towel on chipmakers. Deutsche Bank, for instance, said the group is attractive, especially relative to the software sector.

title: Nasdaq 100 sinks 6% as chipmaker selloff deepens
article:
(Nov 6): A post-election slide in chipmakers snowballed, dragging the Nasdaq 100 down 6%, as investors bailed from the sector on speculation the Democratic sweep in Congress will usher in a new era of regulation for the artificial-intelligence (AI) industry.

The 11% plunge in a gauge of chip giants put the group on track for its worst week since the April 2025 tariff meltdown. Nvidia Corp slid 8%. Qualcomm Inc and Arm Holdings plc’s sank on underwhelming outlooks. Apple Inc plans to raise about US$7 billion from an investment-grade bond sale, adding to a flurry of tech issuance. Tesla Inc and SpaceX each lost 11%. Bitcoin fell 5.5%.

“The rotation out of chipmakers reflects growing concern about the pace and funding of AI spending due to the risk of more regulations after the blue wave, even as earnings remain resilient and valuations have reset sharply,” said Chris Murphy at Susquehanna International Group.

In a rush for safety, defensive industries like consumer staples and healthcare climbed. The swoon in tech shares also lifted bonds despite a rebound in oil prices. Haven currencies including the yen and the Swiss franc outperformed.

The AI trade is here to stay, but it remains volatile, and investors should not overlook some of the more boring areas of the market, according to Bob Edwards at Edwards Asset Management.

See also: Nasdaq 100 sinks 5% as chipmaker sell-off deepens

“We are not concerned about what the blue wave means for the buildout of AI, since the president still has the veto pen and data centres bring jobs and tax revenue,” he said.

Data centres have become an easy political target amid rising electricity bills. Bipartisan energy permitting reform could help by accelerating new power generation and transmission, while politicians will aim to ensure developers pay for the incremental grid infrastructure required to serve them, according to Jordan Jackson and Stephanie Aliaga at JPMorgan Asset Management.

The elections reinforced growing opposition to data centers, particularly in Texas and Ohio, where incoming Democratic governors favour tougher development conditions, they said. However, despite the backlash, statewide moratoriums have struggled to become law, accorrding to the strategists

See also: Krispy Kreme raises revenue outlook as turnaround takes hold

“Politicians may now feel emboldened to adopt a harder stance but face competing pressures to protect ratepayers while attracting jobs, investment and tax revenues. AI remains an evolving public issue and is not yet a clear voter priority,” they noted.
• Microsoft Corp, one of Nscale’s primary customers, opted not to extend a contract at a Texas data centre with the startup ahead of its planned public offering, according to a person familiar with the matter.
• Micron Technology Inc has suspended plans for a memory chip plant in Taiwan due to a protracted labour dispute, according to people familiar with the matter, throwing into question the fate of a major production base for crucial AI components.
• Amazon.com Inc is adding Uber Technologies Inc restaurant delivery perks on its shopping site for Prime members, forging a deeper partnership just a week after rival service DoorDash Inc agreed to acquire Instacart.
• Peloton Interactive Inc forecast holiday-quarter revenue that was slightly above Wall Street’s expectations, even as the fitness company projected a year-over-year sales decline and narrower profit margins.
• Wendy’s Co board unanimously rejected an offer from a group led by Nelson Peltz’s Trian Fund Management to buy out the burger chain for about US$1.4 billion, saying the proposal substantially undervalues the company’s prospects and long-term earnings potential.

Some of the main moves in markets:
• The S&P 500 fell 3.7% as of 10.52am New York time
